lines: An executor pod keeps getting killed, and its own heap metric looks almost calm: about half of what it was allowed.
The engineer's instinct is to give it more memory. Watch what that actually does to how often it gets killed.
It gets killed more often, not less. Something the heap metric never showed is driving this.
Think about what the container's own limit actually counts. It isn't watching the heap specifically, it's watching everything the process touches.
So something took up the other half, and it never shows up on a heap dashboard at all.
Put a name on it.
answer: The JVM's own non-heap memory: metaspace, thread stacks, native buffers, none of them tracked by a heap metric.
A heap ceiling only bounds one part of a process. A container's limit bounds all of it, heap and everything the runtime needs besides.

lines: Follow the limit itself down to where it actually lives: a single file the kernel reads and enforces.
Cross it, and the kernel's own killer steps in. It never asks which kind of memory pushed the process over the line.
That same crossing can end a process three completely different ways, and each one leaves its own signature.
The kernel's own kill ends the whole process outright, no exception thrown, just gone.
A JVM running out of heap raises an error the program can catch and keep running past.
A Python process holding more and more in memory raises nothing at all. It just keeps growing until something else intervenes.
Three deaths, three logs. Guessing which one happened from the symptom alone is how postmortems go wrong.
Here's the part that trips people up about sizing a JVM inside a container: it does read the container's own limit.
But by default, it only reserves a quarter of that limit for the heap itself.
The rest is exactly what the earlier scene was missing: metaspace, thread stacks, native memory, all living outside the heap's own count.
A data engine adds its own overhead on top of whatever memory an executor is given.
For a job running the engine's native runtime, that overhead is a small slice. For a job running another language's runtime underneath it, the slice is four times as large.
Either way, there's a floor beneath it, and heap plus overhead both have to fit inside the one limit the container was actually given.
Now follow the other resource the kernel rations: not memory, but time on the processor.
A quota and a repeating window. Spend the whole quota early in the window, and the kernel holds the process back for whatever's left of it.
That holding-back shows up as its own counted event, visible to anyone who goes looking.
Here's a pod with a processor limit, sitting on a node that otherwise has nothing else running on it.
Is it still throttled, even with the whole node free?
answer: Yes. The limit is measured against the pod's own quota, never against what anyone else on the node is doing.
An idle node changes nothing about a process that asks for more than its own window allows.

lines: Three separate checks watch the same container, and each one answers a different question on failure.
One decides whether to restart it. One decides whether to pull it out of service without touching it. One simply holds the other two back until the slow part finishes.
Skip that last one on a process with a genuinely slow start, and the restart check can trigger before the process ever finishes waking up, restarting something that was never actually stuck.
A limit is a kernel file, not a runtime setting layered on top of it.
Reading it right, and reading the right probe for a slow start, is what the next topic's eviction order and scheduling priority both build on.
